These are census-derived birth years (~1825, ~1828) that are approximate ("~"), and the 1851 and 1861 Residence facts are from the earlier English sources already on the tree before this run — these are not contradictions I introduced. The "contradiction" flags are pre-existing data-quality issues from earlier sourcing, not something the linking I just did created. No new persons were minted (all personas matched existing tree persons). No relationship edges need writing since all family edges already exist in the tree. The 1880 absence of James (I3) and Ellen (I4) is flagged below.

---

Both the 1870 and 1880 Maury County, Tennessee census records have now been linked to the right family members. In 1870, William Weller (head) is matched to William in the tree, Mary to his wife, and their three children James, Ellen, and George are each matched to the corresponding child in the tree — all rated as "probably the same person." In 1880, William and Mary are again found in Maury County, now with only their son George still at home, which again matches the tree. Every match is rated "probably" rather than "certainly" for one reason: the family's move from England to Tennessee, a distance of over 4,200 miles, is not yet explained by any immigration record, passenger list, or naturalization paper in the file, and the FamilySearch Tennessee immigration guide does not identify a recognized corridor for English arrivals to the agricultural South in this period.

Two things stand out that you may want to investigate next: James Weller and Ellen Weller, both present in 1870, are entirely absent from the 1880 census. They may have died in the intervening decade, married and moved away, or been enumerated elsewhere. Finding records for them — or confirming their fates — is the logical next step, alongside searching for any immigration or naturalization record that would account for the family's arrival from England.
